sentences.text: The upland moa belongs to the ratites, a group of flightless birds defined by a sternum that lacks a keel.
This bird lacked wings and a tail.
Unlike other moas, the upland moa had feathers covering its entire body except for the beak and the soles of its feet, an adaptation for cold environments.
Standing less than one meter tall and weighing between 17 and 34 kilograms, the upland moa is one of the smallest known moa species.
The upland moa typically laid only one or two blue-green eggs at a time, likely making it the only moa species to lay non-white eggs.
Richard Owen formally described the upland moa in 1883.
Richard Owen named the species Dinornis didinus in 1883 based on mummified remains discovered in 1878 by H. L. Squires in Queenstown, New Zealand.
Analysis of coprolites suggests the upland moa ate branchlets of trees like Nothofagus, lake-edge herbs, tussock, and nectar-rich flowers.
Similar to emus and ostriches, male upland moas cared for their young.
The upland moa belongs to the parent group Megalapterygidae.
The upland moa is classified in the family Megalapterygidae.
The genus Megalapteryx existed from the Gelasian to the Holocene, spanning from 2.58 to 0 million years ago.
The upland moa inhabited the South Island of New Zealand, primarily favoring alpine and subalpine environments.
The upland moa traveled to elevations as high as 2,000 meters (7,000 feet) above sea level.
The upland moa became extinct around 1500 CE following hunting by the Māori.
A 2005 genetic study suggested that Megalapteryx benhami might be a valid species rather than a junior synonym of M. didinus.
